US banks limit AI agents’ access to customer accounts – report
Vidhya Edwards Munnangi
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 6:32 AM CDT 2 min read
C
BAC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Citigroup and Bank of America are restricting AI agents from accessing customer accounts, joining JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab in tightening controls over automated financial tools, reported the Financial Times.

Banks fear agents will drain deposits by shifting idle cash to higher returns, the report noted.

Citi does not permit "third-party AI agents or assistants to log into a customer's account or transact directly within our digital banking platforms".

The restriction was intended to protect customer accounts and information.

Bank of America is limiting AI agents' access to consumer deposits, according to a person familiar with the matter.

Chief executive Brian Moynihan said the bank was developing protocols to determine which party would be liable for payments authorised by AI.

"We strongly believe there should be a human in the loop to authorise money moving out of your account," Moynihan told CNBC.

According to sources, Wall Street executives have contacted Federal Reserve regulators about the growing use of AI agents for financial transactions.

Regulators have privately supported banks' decisions to block AI agents from client accounts, the news publication added.

Officials believe the law may need to clarify how customers authorise autonomous technology to act on their behalf, and who is liable if a transaction fails or causes a loss.

JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon said this week that the bank would limit AI agents' access to client accounts "because you don't want rogue agents and there could be thousands of them".

"We have to make sure we protect our customers in the right way. So, we're building tools to do that, too," Dimon said on the bank's third-quarter results call.

Charles Schwab chief executive Rick Wurster told Bloomberg that the brokerage, wealth-management, and banking company was blocking unauthorised AI agents attempting to transfer clients' money, including Meta Platforms' Muse.

"US banks limit AI agents' access to customer accounts – report" was originally created and published by Retail Banker International, a GlobalData owned brand.

JPMorgan JPM has sharply reduced its share repurchases, signaling a strategic shift toward reinvesting capital in its businesses. The banking giant reported net share buybacks of just $664 million in the third quarter of 2026, down nearly 89% from $6.2 billion in the preceding quarter.

CEO Jamie Dimon emphasized that investing in JPMorgan's franchise and supporting clients remain higher priorities than repurchasing shares. With approximately $30 billion in excess capital, the bank sees opportunities to deploy funds into businesses capable of generating attractive long-term returns.

The strategy appears promising, given JPMorgan's diversified operations and strong market position. Investments in technology, branch expansion, commercial banking, wealth management and international operations could strengthen customer relationships and support sustainable revenue growth. Rising demand for financing across infrastructure and other capital-intensive sectors presents additional opportunities for business expansion.

JPMorgan's financial strength provides considerable flexibility. The bank ended the third quarter with $304 billion in Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital and a standardized CET1 ratio of 13.9%. Its profitability also remained robust, with a return on tangible common equity of 20%.

However, fewer buybacks may limit near-term earnings growth, while the higher 2026 adjusted expense outlook of $108.6 billion underscores cost pressures. Returns on investments may also take time to materialize. Nevertheless, JPMorgan's capital allocation strategy appears prudent. Prioritizing high-return growth opportunities over repurchases at elevated valuations could strengthen its competitive position and create greater long-term shareholder value.

Citigroup and Bank of America in Terms of Q3 Share Buybacks

Citigroup C repurchased approximately $3 billion of shares in the third quarter of 2026, bringing year-to-date buybacks to $13.3 billion. As of Sept. 30, 2026, $23 billion worth of shares remained available under the share repurchase program. 

Citigroup returned $4.1 billion to shareholders, including dividends, reflecting its continued focus on capital distributions alongside investments in business growth and improving profitability.

Bank of America BAC repurchased $6 billion worth of shares during third-quarter 2026, reflecting its commitment to shareholder returns. As of Sept. 30, 2026, almost $11 billion remained under its $40 billion share repurchase authorization. 

Including $2.2 billion in dividends, Bank of America returned $8.3 billion to shareholders. The buybacks highlight management's confidence in its capital position, supported by a solid CET1 ratio of 10.9%.

title: Citi’s Manthey Sees French Equities Volatile Beyond April Vote
detail:
Citi’s Manthey Sees French Equities Volatile Beyond April Vote
Bloomberg · Bloomberg
Matt Clinch, Anna Edwards, Guy Johnson and Tom Mackenzie
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 4:51 AM CDT 2 min read
C
Trade C on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

(Bloomberg) -- France's political risk won't end with April's presidential election, according to Citigroup Inc.'s Beata Manthey, who says the bigger test for markets is whether any government can command a parliamentary majority and deliver a credible path to lower debt.

Most Read from Bloomberg

Zelenskyy Says Trump Is Pushing Ukraine, Not Putin, to Yield

White House Turmoil Erupts as Trump Axes Zacharia, Backs Wiles

Sydney's New $4 Billion Airport Opens With Barely Any Flights

Trump Faces Midterm Fuel Reckoning as Gas Prices Near Biden's Average

Stocks Rebound From Chip Rout as Earnings Await: Markets Wrap

Manthey, Citi's head of European equity strategy, said the prolonged uncertainty stems from the structure of French politics. Markets will need to see whether in the wake of the ballot, the government can secure a parliamentary majority to propose a fiscal plan that leads to lower debt.

"Our view is that French equities are going to be more volatile," she said in a Bloomberg Television interview. "And the situation is not going to be resolved until the summer probably."

Despite the turbulence, Citi's stance on France is neutral, with the wider European continent also rated neutral in a global context, on the view that a lot of the bad news is already priced in.

Manthey noted that investor anxiety about France tends to spread broadly, with French bank moves tracking sovereign spreads and rippling into wider European equity indexes.

She said that if the fiscal situation gets further out of hand, higher sovereign spreads would translate directly into a deeper selloff in French bank valuations. She added it remains risky to short French equities at current levels as prices will be "oscillating up and down."

The assessment comes after a weekend of political turbulence in France that Manthey said added another layer of complexity to an already fragile situation. Cost-of-living protests gathered more than half a million people in France, before degenerating into looting and burning.

French government bonds underperformed most European peers Monday, causing the spread between its 10-year yield and the German equivalent to widen seven basis points to 145 basis points. The euro fell as much as 0.5%. French equities also underperformed, with the CAC 40 index falling 1.2% while the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropped 0.7%.

Best Q3 in a decade

C Stock Price: 1-Year (TIKR)

Citigroup (C:NYSE) stock is up 29% over the past year, closing at $124.26 on October 16, but the most recent stretch of that year has gone the wrong way. On October 13, Citi beat third-quarter estimates and the stock fell anyway, dropping 5.6% to $124.53. It was the second post-earnings slide in three months.

Citigroup stock closed 2025 at $116.69, so its 2026 gain is just 6.5% by my math, and the shares sit 11.2% below their June 30 close of $139.96. The business kept improving the whole time.

Citigroup Stock Did Its Climbing Before July

The 29% return puts the starting point in mid-October 2025 at $96.25, so the stock gained 21% before 2025 ended. The first quarter took some of that back: by March 14, Citi traded at $105.69, down 9.4% for the year amid fears over the Middle East conflict.

On April 14, Citi reported first-quarter EPS of $3.06 against a $2.65 estimate. At its May 7 Investor Day, it set an 11% to 13% target for return on tangible common equity in 2027 and 2028 and announced a $30 billion buyback. Return on tangible common equity (RoTCE) measures profit against shareholders' capital, excluding goodwill. After a late-June peak in the mid-$140s, Citigroup stock closed June at $139.96.

Two Earnings Beats, Two Drops for C Stock

The giveback started on July 14. Citi posted second-quarter EPS of $3.15 and revenue of $24.77 billion, the highest quarterly revenue in a decade, with RoTCE of 13%. But it kept its full-year RoTCE target at 10% to 11% and said it could pull forward investments planned for later years, and Citigroup stock fell 5.3% that day.

It closed September at $129.48, then fell as much as 4.6% intraday on October 1 as steadily rising Treasury yields pulled bank stocks lower.

The October 13 report beat on the headline and slowed underneath it:

EPS came in at $2.85 against the $2.66 analysts expected, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters, and revenue rose 8% to $23.8 billion, Citi's best third quarter in a decade.

RoTCE slipped to 11.5% from 13.0% in the second quarter, Markets revenue fell 13% sequentially to $6.1 billion, and management expected a seasonal fourth-quarter Markets revenue decline of about 20% from the third quarter, "or possibly a bit more."

title: Citigroup: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Citigroup: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors
The Motley Fool Team, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 12:20 PM CDT 3 min read
C
Trade C on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

On its third quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 13, 2026, Citigroup (NYSE:C) reported net income of $5.2 billion. The bank's continuing structural overhaul cuts corporate overhead expenses to fund artificial intelligence upgrades and expand high-return corporate services. Three takeaways from management's comments stand out for long-term investors.

1. Severance Charges Fund Structural Cost Reductions and Technology

Management is trimming headcount across corporate functions to eliminate redundant expenses. Reinvesting those severance savings, which are job-termination payouts to outgoing staff, into modern technology platforms creates operational capacity for future business growth.

On a year to date basis, we have recognized over $1 billion of severance, largely across functions, technology and operations as we continue to drive structural efficiencies and bring down transformation expenses and stranded costs to create capacity for business growth.
-- Gonzalo Luchetti, Chief Financial Officer

2. Artificial Intelligence Tools Actively Reduce Software Vendor Expenses

Internal deployment of automated coding software helps engineering teams to complete technical projects in-house rather than outsourcing work. That shift lowers external software supplier costs while accelerating product rollouts for corporate clients.

We have reduced our tech vendor spend by 30% year over year as a consequence, and that is still got a long way to run.
-- Jane Nind Fraser, Chair and Chief Executive Officer

3. Asset Inflows Accelerate Fee Growth Across Wealth Management

Net new investment assets, which represent fresh capital brought in by wealth clients, doubled year over year. There was also strong uptake among retail clients who transitioned to wealth products. Expanding client accounts builds steady fee streams that protect profitability against fluctuating interest rates.

We brought in $38 billion in net new investment assets this quarter, up over 100% from a year ago.
-- Jane Nind Fraser, Chair and Chief Executive Officer

Looking Ahead

Third-quarter revenue expanded 8% year over year as execution gained traction across global services and consumer cards segments. A global institutional network, blockchain and payment tokenization for digital assets growing to seven markets, and automated risk systems build operational scale. Management is watching trading seasonality, deposit competition, and capital regulation changes.

Our strategy is working, and we have a clear path to delivering higher, sustainable returns.
-- Gonzalo Luchetti, Chief Financial Officer
